issues.legal_issue: A prior judgment directing a public authority to reconsider and decide an application according to law does not bar a later decision on the application when the earlier judgment did not finally determine the controversy.
material_facts: In an earlier writ proceeding, the court directed the Municipal Council to dispose of the construction-permission application according to law without deciding its merits.
A later resolution to replan the scheme had been passed while that proceeding was pending, but it was not brought to the court’s attention.
The Council later rejected the application on the basis of the replanning resolution, and that rejection was challenged in a subsequent writ proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgment did not finally decide the controversy, so res judicata did not prevent the Municipal Council from reconsidering and deciding the application.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata requires a final decision of the controversy. A direction to reconsider and dispose of an application according to law, without determining its merits, leaves the matter open. The Court applied the principle of res judicata, including the asserted doctrine of constructive res judicata, and relied on no specific provision or earlier case.

predicates.subsequent_writ_challenges_public_author: A party brought a later writ proceeding challenging a public authority’s decision on an application.
predicates.earlier_judgment_directed_lawful_reconsi: An earlier judgment directed the public authority to reconsider and decide the application according to law.
predicates.earlier_judgment_did_not_decide_merits: The earlier judgment did not determine the merits of the application or finally resolve the controversy.

issues.definition: When a later writ challenges a public authority’s decision, an earlier direction to reconsider according to law does not bar the later decision if the earlier judgment left the merits unresolved.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority’s earlier resolution granting permission does not prevent it from later changing its decision when the resolution was not a binding compromise.
material_facts: The Municipal Council passed a resolution deciding to grant construction permission.
The applicant later withdrew a damages suit, but the evidence did not establish that the resolution resulted from a compromise between the parties.
The State Government required the Council to explain the matter, appointed a committee to examine it, and the Council later rescinded the resolution.
issues.conclusion: The earlier resolution was not a binding compromise and did not disable the Municipal Council from taking a different decision later.
issues.legal_principle: The withdrawal of a suit after a favourable resolution does not, by itself, establish a binding compromise or make the resolution irrevocable. A municipal body performing public duties remains answerable to the State Government and may later take a different decision. The Court relied on no specific provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

rule.if: public_authority_decision_is_challenged and earlier_resolution_favoured_applicant and applicant_withdrew_suit_after_resolution and no_binding_compromise_established

predicates.public_authority_decision_is_challenged: A party challenged a public authority’s later decision concerning an earlier resolution.
predicates.earlier_resolution_favoured_applicant: A public authority earlier passed a resolution in favour of the applicant.
predicates.applicant_withdrew_suit_after_resolution: The applicant withdrew a suit after the favourable resolution was passed.
predicates.no_binding_compromise_established: The facts do not establish that the earlier resolution resulted from a binding compromise between the parties.

issues.definition: An earlier favourable resolution does not prevent a public authority from deciding differently later when no binding compromise was established, even if the applicant withdrew a suit after the resolution.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority entrusted with community needs may modify or replace a public scheme as circumstances and public requirements change.
material_facts: Land previously considered for construction permission was later identified for public purposes connected with traffic circulation and road widening.
A committee reported that the land would be needed for proper traffic circulation.
The Municipal Council resolved to replan the scheme, invite objections, and later rejected the construction application on the basis of the revised scheme.
issues.conclusion: The Municipal Council could modify or substitute the scheme to meet changing public needs, and the earlier favourable resolution did not make the land permanently unavailable for another public purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a statutory scheme serves the public interest must be assessed according to the needs of the time. Community requirements change, so a public authority entrusted with those requirements may periodically vary or replace a scheme. The Court referred generally to statutory provisions and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, section 4, in the case background, but cited no earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: public_scheme_decision_is_challenged and public_authority_has_duty_to_assess_community_needs and community_needs_have_changed and revised_scheme_serves_public_purpose

predicates.public_scheme_decision_is_challenged: A party challenged a public authority’s decision concerning a public scheme.
predicates.public_authority_has_duty_to_assess_comm: The public authority is entrusted with looking after the requirements of the community.
predicates.community_needs_have_changed: The requirements of the community have changed since the scheme or earlier decision was made.
predicates.revised_scheme_serves_public_purpose: The revised scheme is intended to serve a public purpose in response to those requirements.

issues.definition: A public authority entrusted with community needs may modify or replace a challenged scheme when those needs have changed and the revised scheme serves a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: An allegation that a public authority acted mala fide cannot be accepted without material supporting it.
material_facts: The respondent alleged that the authorities acted mala fide at the instance of other respondents.
The High Court had made no finding of mala fides.
The Supreme Court found no material supporting the allegation.
issues.conclusion: The allegation of mala fides was unsupported and did not provide a basis to disturb the authority’s decision.
issues.legal_principle: A claim of mala fides requires supporting material; the Court found none and relied on no specific provision or earlier case.

predicates.public_authority_decision_is_challenged: A party challenged a decision made by a public authority.
predicates.mala_fides_are_alleged: The challenger alleged that the public authority acted with improper intent.
predicates.no_material_supports_mala_fides: The record contains no material supporting the allegation of improper intent.

issues.definition: When mala fides are alleged in a challenge to a public authority’s decision, the allegation is not established if the record contains no supporting material.
